stem_html:
In her study of Baroque altarpieces, Mendoza argues that Caravaggio's compositions ______ the viewer's eye rather than guiding it. A shaft of light lands on a hand or a heel and holds the gaze there, so that the narrative reaches us out of order, in fragments the viewer has to reassemble without help from the painter.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The familiar collocation. “Captivate the eye” is the phrase that comes to mind first, and it is the wrong one here. The sentence is not about how appealing the paintings are; it is about motion being stopped.
  • Reading the contrast backwards. The blank is defined by “rather than guiding it,” so the answer has to be the opposite of guiding, not a different direction of guiding.
  • Filling the blank from the first sentence. Under time pressure the second sentence never gets read, and the second sentence is where all the evidence is.

Why A is right To arrest is to bring to a stop. The next sentence says a shaft of light lands on a hand or a heel and holds the gaze there, which is motion halted at one point — exactly what “rather than guiding” sets up as the alternative.

Why B is wrong Captivate says the eye is attracted and held pleasurably, but it carries no sense of interruption, and an eye can be captivated while being led. It also imports an judgement of the painting's charm that Mendoza never makes.

Why C is wrong Divert means to send elsewhere, which is still a way of directing the eye. The contrast in the sentence rules out any answer that keeps the eye travelling.

Why D is wrong Obscure would mean the paintings hide their subjects. The passage says the opposite: the light makes one detail intensely visible. What the viewer lacks is order, not visibility.

The fragments reach the viewer out of order precisely because the eye is stopped rather than led.

stem_html:
Reviewers of Okonkwo's first novel were ______: they praised its structure at length, noted its dialogue only in passing, and declined to compare the book with the work of her contemporaries — an omission that, in a field where such comparisons are routine, readers took as a verdict of its own.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two thirds of the sentence looks like silence. Two of the three clauses describe things the reviewers did not do, which pulls hard toward a word meaning “said little.” The first clause says they praised its structure at length.
  • The intensity trap. The sentence describes withheld praise, not attack. Choosing a word at the wrong strength is the most common miss on this question type.
  • A near-synonym that means something else. “Equivocal” sounds like withholding but names ambiguity, and nothing here is ambiguous.

Why A is wrong Reticent means unwilling to speak. Reviewers who praised its structure at length were not reticent; they were selective about what they praised.

Why B is right Guarded describes praise that is real but deliberately limited: extensive on one point, glancing on a second, absent on a third. It fits all three clauses at once, which no other choice does.

Why C is wrong Dismissive is too strong. A dismissive reviewer does not praise a book's structure at length, and the passage records genuine praise, only fenced in.

Why D is wrong Equivocal means open to two readings. These reviews were not ambiguous; readers understood the omission perfectly well, which is the point of the final clause.

stem_html:
Because the interferometer could not ______ features separated by less than half a wavelength, the team could report only that the two stars lay within 0.4 arcseconds of each other; whether the light came from two objects or three stayed an open question for another decade.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The everyday sense of a technical word. “Resolve” most often means to settle a dispute, and the sentence ends on an unsettled question, so the wrong sense is primed twice over.
  • Detecting and separating are different failures. The instrument saw the light. What it could not do was tell two sources apart.

Why A is right In optics, to resolve is to distinguish two close sources as separate. That is exactly the stated limit: the team could report only that the two stars lay within 0.4 arcseconds of each other, and could not say how many objects the light came from.

Why B is wrong Detect fails on the evidence. The stars were observed and a separation of 0.4 arcseconds was measured, so detection succeeded where separation did not.

Why C is wrong Settle is the courtroom sense of resolve, and an instrument does not settle features. The unresolved question at the end of the sentence is what makes this tempting, and it is a consequence of the limit rather than the limit itself.

Why D is wrong Magnification and resolution are different things: enlarging a blur produces a bigger blur. Nothing in the sentence concerns image size.

stem_html:
A researcher studying urban crows claimed that the birds' habit of dropping walnuts onto crosswalks spreads by imitation rather than by independent invention. She noted that in Sendai the behavior appeared in one park in 1997 and was recorded in every adjacent park within four years, while no population more than twenty kilometers away performed it before 2004. A skeptic replied that the timing is equally consistent with each population inventing the behavior once local traffic passed a threshold, and pointed out that traffic in the outlying districts reached the 1997 Sendai level only in 2003.

Which finding, if true, would most directly undermine the skeptic's objection?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Two outlying districts whose traffic passed the 1997 Sendai level in 1999 recorded no walnut-dropping until Sendai crows were observed visiting them in 2004."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Traffic in Sendai's central parks continued to rise after 1997, and walnut-dropping there became more frequent every year.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Crows in every population studied are capable of learning novel foraging behaviors by watching other crows.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "No population has ever been observed dropping walnuts onto a road that carries no traffic.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Answering the wrong question. The task is to undermine the skeptic, not to support the researcher in general. Three choices are friendly to the imitation thesis in a loose way and do nothing at all to the objection.
  • Capacity mistaken for cause. Showing that crows can imitate never shows that here they did. Both explanations assume capable birds.
  • Date-matching under time pressure. The passage hands you 1997, 2003 and 2004 on purpose, and a student skimming takes whichever choice repeats a year.

Why A is right The skeptic's claim is that the traffic threshold alone explains the timing. A names districts that crossed that threshold in 1999 and still produced no walnut-dropping until contact with Sendai crows in 2004: the threshold was met and the behavior did not appear, so the threshold is not sufficient. That is the objection's load-bearing assumption removed.

Why B is wrong It reports that an established behavior intensified where it already existed. Both explanations predict that, so it separates nothing.

Why C is wrong Capacity, not cause. A universal ability to imitate is exactly as compatible with each population inventing the behavior independently.

Why D is wrong This confirms that traffic is necessary, which is the skeptic's own premise. Strengthening the objection is the reverse of undermining it.

stem_html:
Soil scientists tested whether adding biochar raises the water held by sandy soils. Four plots received biochar at different rates, and the team measured the water retained after a fixed drying period. The team concluded that retention rises with the application rate only up to a point, beyond which further biochar adds nothing.

Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the team's conclusion?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Retention rose from 8% at 0 tons per hectare to 17% at 5 tons, and rose again to 22% at 10 tons.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Doubling the application from 10 to 20 tons per hectare raised retention only from 22% to 22.6%, while the first 10 tons raised it from 8% to 22%."}, {"letter": "C", "content": "The plot receiving 20 tons per hectare retained more water than any other plot tested.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Retention at 20 tons per hectare was nearly three times the retention of the untreated plot.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Reading the graph correctly and still answering wrongly. Every choice states a true number. Only one of them is evidence for a ceiling, and a ceiling is what the conclusion asserts.
  • The rising half of the data. Choice A quotes the interval where the effect is real, which is the part of the chart the eye lands on first, and it is the half that argues against the conclusion.
  • Biggest is not the same as still growing. The last bar being tallest is equally compatible with a ceiling and with unlimited growth.

Why A is wrong It reports only the stretch in which retention was still climbing steeply. That supports “biochar works,” not “the effect stops,” and it is the strongest distractor precisely because every number in it is right.

Why B is right A conclusion about diminishing returns needs two intervals compared. Doubling the dose from 10 to 20 tons buys 0.6 of a percentage point where the first 10 tons bought 14. Only this choice puts the two side by side, which is what “up to a point, beyond which further biochar adds nothing” claims.

Why C is wrong True and unhelpful. The 20-ton plot would also be the highest if retention were still rising steeply, so this cannot tell the team's conclusion apart from its opposite.

Why D is wrong This compares the treated extreme with the untreated control, which supports the general effectiveness of biochar. The conclusion is about what happens at the top of the range, not about whether biochar does anything at all.

stem_html:
In 1919 the physician Marion Hale reported that a hospital ward whose windows were opened each morning had one third the influenza transmission of a sealed ward in the same building, and she attributed the difference to ventilation. Later historians noted that the open ward was also the ward to which convalescent patients were moved once they were judged out of danger.

Which finding would most strongly support the historians' implied criticism of Hale's conclusion?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Air exchange in the open ward was measured at roughly four times that of the sealed ward.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Patients transferred to the open ward had on average been symptomatic for nine days, past the interval in which the virus is usually transmitted."}, {"letter": "C", "content": "The sealed ward was more crowded than the open ward throughout the outbreak.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Hale did not record the ages of the patients on either ward.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A second flaw is not the flaw asked about. Crowding and missing ages are both real weaknesses in the study, and neither is the historians' point, which is specifically about who was moved to the open ward.
  • Supporting the original claim by accident. Choice A measures the very mechanism Hale proposed. A student who reads “support” and loses track of whose argument is being supported takes it.
  • Absence of data feels damning. A missing variable sounds fatal but establishes nothing on its own.

Why A is wrong Confirming that the open ward really was better ventilated strengthens Hale. The question asks for support of the criticism.

Why B is right The historians' observation is that convalescent patients were moved once they were judged out of danger, so the open ward held people selected for being further along in their illness. B supplies what that observation needs in order to become an objection: those patients were past the infectious window, so the ward's low transmission is explained by whom it held rather than by its air.

Why C is wrong Crowding is a genuine confounder, but it is a different one and not the one the historians noted. It also tends to travel with poor ventilation, so it does not cleanly separate the two explanations.

Why D is wrong An unrecorded variable is a gap in the record, not evidence that the conclusion is wrong, and nothing in the passage suggests the wards differed by age.

stem_html:
In Toshiko Aoyama's short story “The Lacquer Box,” a daughter returns to sort her late mother's belongings. A critic argues that the story withholds the daughter's grief from the reader by displacing it onto the handling of objects.

Which quotation from “The Lacquer Box” most effectively illustrates the critic's claim?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "“She wept then, quietly, in the way her mother had taught her to weep, which was not to be heard.”", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "“She turned the box over twice, set it down, picked it up again, and only then noticed she had been holding it long enough for the lacquer to warm.”"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "“The apartment was smaller than she remembered, and the window faced a wall that had not been there before.”", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "“Grief, she decided, was a kind of inventory: everything counted twice and nothing accounted for.”", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The word in the claim appears in a choice. D contains “grief” and even defines it, which makes it magnetic, and stating the emotion outright is the opposite of withholding it.
  • Showing the emotion versus displacing it. A depicts the daughter crying, which is the feeling on the page rather than moved off it.
  • Atmosphere read as evidence. C describes objects, but no feeling is being carried by them.

Why A is wrong The daughter weeps. The critic's claim is that the story keeps her grief away from the reader, so a direct depiction of weeping refutes the claim rather than illustrating it.

Why B is right Nothing is said about how she feels. The feeling is legible only in what her hands do — turning, setting down, picking up — and in the detail that enough time passed for the lacquer to warm without her noticing. That is emotion displaced onto the handling of objects, which is the critic's claim exactly.

Why C is wrong This is setting. It reports the room's size and the view, and no object is being handled in a way that carries feeling.

Why D is wrong It names grief and analyses it in the daughter's own voice. An aphorism is the most exposed form of interior life the story could offer, not a withholding of it.

stem_html:
The Antikythera mechanism—a corroded bronze device of at least thirty gears, recovered from a Roman-era shipwreck in 1901______ its front dial tracks the sun and moon against the zodiac, and its back dials predict eclipses decades in advance.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "—is the earliest known analog computer:"}, {"letter": "B", "content": ", is the earliest known analog computer,", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "—is the earliest known analog computer,", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "is the earliest known analog computer:", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The pair that has to match. The interruption opens with a dash, so it has to close with a dash. Every wrong choice here closes it with the wrong mark or does not close it at all.
  • Distance hides the error. Fifteen words separate the opening dash from the blank, and by the time a reader arrives the opening punctuation has been forgotten.
  • A comma in front of an independent clause. What follows the blank could stand alone as a sentence, so a comma there is a splice, and it reads perfectly naturally aloud, which is what makes it dangerous.

Why A is right The dash closes the pair opened before “a corroded bronze device,” and the colon introduces the explanation of what the mechanism does. Both marks are doing work no other mark can do here.

Why B is wrong A comma cannot close an interruption that a dash opened, and it also puts a comma in front of the independent clause that follows.

Why C is wrong The dash correctly closes the pair, and then the comma joins two independent clauses with no conjunction. Because the first half of this choice is right, it is the one most often chosen.

Why D is wrong The interruption is never closed, so the appositive runs straight into the main verb and the sentence loses track of its subject.

stem_html:
Marine biologist René Hurtado spent three seasons recording the clicks of sperm whales off Dominica______ recordings revealed that each family group uses a distinct pattern of clicks, a kind of dialect passed from mothers to calves.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A conjunction that flattens the logic. Choice A is grammatical. It is still wrong for this sentence, because “and” presents the finding as a second event rather than as what the three seasons produced — and a question that has one grammatical distractor is where most points are lost.
  • A demonstrative used as glue. “These” after a comma feels like a connector and is really the subject of a new sentence, which makes it a splice.
  • Fused clauses read fluently. Choice D omits punctuation altogether, and read aloud at speed the sentence sounds finished.

Why A is wrong Comma plus “and” does join two independent clauses correctly, so this is the trap: it is punctuated legally and reported as merely additive, which loses the sentence's actual relation, that the recordings are the result of the three seasons.

Why B is wrong “, these recordings revealed” joins two independent clauses with a comma. A textbook splice, and the most chosen wrong answer because “these” feels like it points back rather than starting over.

Why C is right Two independent clauses, closely related, joined by a semicolon. The second clause reports what the recording produced, which is exactly the relation a semicolon marks without spelling it out.

Why D is wrong With no punctuation the clauses fuse: “off Dominica recordings revealed” reads briefly as a single clause, which is why the error survives a quick read.

stem_html:
What the excavation at Göbekli Tepe overturned was not the dating of monumental architecture______ the assumption that people had to settle and farm before they could build on that scale.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": ", but rather"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "; but rather", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": " but, rather", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}, {"letter": "D", "content": ": but rather", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Not X but Y” is one structure, not two sentences. What follows the blank is a noun phrase with no verb of its own, so every mark that requires an independent clause to its right is out.
  • Length disguises shape. Strip the modifiers and the sentence is “What the excavation overturned was not the dating but the assumption.” Most of the wrong choices become obviously impossible once it is that short.

Why A is right A comma is the standard mark inside a “not X, but rather Y” correlative, and Y here is a noun phrase completing the same predicate.

Why B is wrong A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and “but rather the assumption that people had to settle and farm” has no verb of its own.

Why C is wrong This fences off “rather” instead of marking the contrast, so the adverb is separated from the conjunction it modifies and the required pause before “but” goes unmarked.

Why D is wrong A colon introduces an explanation or a list and cannot be followed by a coordinating conjunction. What makes it tempting is that the second half genuinely does explain the first.

stem_html:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The vaquita is a porpoise found only in the northern Gulf of California.
  • A 2023 acoustic survey estimated that between 6 and 8 individuals remained.
  • Vaquitas drown in gillnets set illegally for the totoaba fish.
  • The 2023 survey recorded calves alongside adults.
  • Genetic modeling published in 2022 found that the species carries little of the harmful variation that usually dooms small populations.

The student wants to emphasize a reason for cautious optimism about the vaquita. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "The vaquita, a porpoise found only in the northern Gulf of California, drowns in gillnets set illegally for the totoaba fish.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Although a 2023 survey estimated that only 6 to 8 vaquitas remained, it recorded calves among them, and genetic modeling suggests the species lacks the harmful variation that usually dooms small populations."}, {"letter": "C", "content": "A 2023 acoustic survey estimated that between 6 and 8 vaquitas remained in the northern Gulf of California.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Genetic modeling published in 2022 examined the harmful variation carried by the vaquita, a porpoise of the northern Gulf of California.", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Accuracy is not the bar. All four choices are faithful to the notes. Only one does the stated job, and the job is the whole question.
  • The most dramatic note is the wrong note. “6 to 8 individuals” is the fact that sticks, and on its own it argues for despair.
  • Naming a study is not reporting its finding. D mentions the genetic modeling without saying what it found, so the optimism never arrives.

Why A is wrong This states the threat. It is relevant to the vaquita's plight and directly opposed to the goal of conveying optimism.

Why B is right Two notes are grounds for hope: the survivors are still reproducing, and the population is not carrying the genetic load that usually finishes a species this small. B uses both, and it concedes the low count instead of hiding it, which is what makes the optimism cautious rather than empty.

Why C is wrong A bare estimate of 6 to 8 is the bleakest fact in the notes, and it is chosen under time pressure because it is the most memorable one.

Why D is wrong It reports that modeling was done and describes the animal, but never states the result. A study that “examined the harmful variation” could as easily have found a great deal of it.

stem_html:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Ceramicist Toshiko Takaezu made closed forms: vessels sealed except for a small opening.
  • She placed a bead of clay inside many of them before sealing them.
  • The bead makes a sound when the piece is moved.
  • Museums display the pieces on plinths, where visitors cannot lift them.
  • Takaezu called the sealed interior “the part that belongs to the pot.”

The student wants to explain a tension between how the works were made and how they are exhibited. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Takaezu, who made closed forms sealed except for a small opening, called the sealed interior “the part that belongs to the pot.”", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Takaezu sealed a bead of clay inside many of her closed forms so that they sound when moved, yet museums display the pieces on plinths, where visitors cannot lift them."}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Museums display Takaezu's closed forms on plinths, where visitors cannot lift them.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Because Takaezu's closed forms are sealed except for a small opening, the interior of each one is hidden from view.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • One side of a tension is not a tension. C gives only the display convention and D only a fact about the making. Each is half the answer and each reads as complete.
  • The quotation is bait. A quoted phrase from the artist feels like the most authoritative material available, and this one addresses neither making nor exhibiting.

Why A is wrong The quotation is about the artist's idea of the interior. Nothing in it concerns how the works are shown, so no tension is set up.

Why B is right A tension needs both halves and a connective. B gives the making, a bead sealed inside so the piece sounds when moved, then the exhibition practice that puts that sound out of reach, joined by “yet.”

Why C is wrong The exhibition half alone. Without the bead, a plinth is simply how ceramics are shown and nothing is in conflict with it.

Why D is wrong Hiddenness from view is not what the plinth prevents. The notes make the conflict about sound and handling, not about sight.

stem_html:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Lidar surveys of the Mosquitia region of Honduras were flown in 2012.
  • The surveys mapped earthworks under a dense forest canopy.
  • Press coverage described the find as a “lost city.”
  • Archaeologists working in the region had recorded surface features there since the 1990s.
  • Lidar measured the extent of the earthworks in weeks rather than decades.

The student wants to make and support a claim about what lidar contributed. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Lidar did not discover the Mosquitia earthworks, which archaeologists had recorded from the surface since the 1990s; what it contributed was measurement of their extent in weeks rather than decades."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Lidar surveys flown over the Mosquitia region of Honduras in 2012 mapped earthworks under a dense forest canopy.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Press coverage of the 2012 lidar surveys described the Mosquitia earthworks as a “lost city,” a phrase archaeologists who had worked in the region since the 1990s would dispute.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Because a dense forest canopy covers the Mosquitia region, archaeologists recorded surface features there for two decades before lidar was flown in 2012.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A claim needs a predicate the notes can defend. B is a summary of what happened rather than an assertion about what the technology contributed, and a summary is easy to mistake for a claim.
  • The quotable note pulls hardest. “Lost city” is the most vivid item, and a choice built on it argues about press language instead of about lidar.
  • Invented causation. D makes the canopy the reason archaeologists worked from the surface, which the notes never say.

Why A is right It states a claim — lidar's contribution was speed and scale, not discovery — and supports both halves from the notes: the surface record going back to the 1990s, and the weeks-not-decades measurement.

Why B is wrong Every word is accurate and nothing is claimed. It reports the survey and stops, which leaves the goal of making and supporting a claim unmet.

Why C is wrong This is a claim about journalism. The goal names lidar's contribution, and a dispute over the phrase “lost city” is about how the find was described.

Why D is wrong It invents a causal link the notes do not contain and, in doing so, says nothing about what lidar added.
